provenance.note: Envelope lists the registered upstreams; every fact carries its own citation (source_label/source_url/data_date), including one-off documents (ASI monuments, the 1994 MoU, CWC case studies, court reporting) not registrable as living sources. note: Hand-curated quotable facts for /delhi/facts (static pipeline). Every fact carries its own source; figures follow the 2026-07-20 verification refresh of the Delhi audit (37 STPs not 40; Najafgarh Jheel 226 sq km; AKTC 2007-2020 core phase). The Sept 2025 Hathnikund peak is deliberately EXCLUDED pending resolution of the 3,29,313 (SANDRP) vs 29,313 (DD News) discrepancy. Hindi renderings land with the translation pass.

facts.title: India's oldest surviving gravity dam is in the Delhi ridge
facts.unit: century CE (Tomara dynasty)
facts.interpretation: The Anangpur bund - 101 m of dressed-quartzite gravity dam across a ridge stream south of Delhi - still stands from Tomara times, the head of a hydraulic chain (Anangpur -> Surajkund -> Tughlaqabad's fortress baolis) that makes Delhi the longest continuously engineered water landscape of any Indian metropolis. Not 4th-century-BCE as sometimes claimed; the microlith finds nearby are older than the dam.

facts.title: Hauz-i-Shamsi: a Sultanate reservoir in use since 1230
facts.unit: CE (Iltutmish)
facts.interpretation: Sultan Iltutmish's royal tank at Mehrauli predates Hauz Khas by over a century and still holds water - a working artefact of the talab-hauz-baoli system that watered Delhi for six centuries before piped supply.

facts.title: Hauz Khas was a ~50-hectare royal water tank
facts.unit: CE (Firuz Shah Tughlaq's restoration)
facts.interpretation: Built under Alauddin Khalji for Siri and restored by Firuz Shah Tughlaq, the 'royal tank' originally spread over roughly 50 hectares (600 x 700 m, ~4 m deep). Today's lake is a fragment - but it is one of the only Sultanate tanks still wet.

facts.title: Shahjahanabad drank from a canal called the Stream of Paradise
facts.unit: CE (Nahar-i-Behisht)
facts.interpretation: Ali Mardan Khan's revival of Firuz Shah's canal carried Yamuna water ~130 km from the north into Shah Jahan's new capital, feeding the Red Fort and Chandni Chowk's central channel. The British dismantled it after 1857 - the moment Delhi stopped storing and channelling its own water.
facts.source_label: Sahapedia - Traditional Water Systems of Delhi

facts.title: Delhi still holds an entire museum of stepwells
facts.unit: surviving baolis (ASI-protected + INTACH-documented)
facts.interpretation: From Agrasen ki Baoli in the CBD to the Mehrauli cluster (Rajon, Gandhak) and Tughlaqabad's fortress wells, Delhi's surviving stepwells span a millennium of groundwater engineering; INTACH and Google Arts & Culture have digitised seven of them.
facts.source_label: INTACH x Google Arts & Culture - Baolis of Delhi

facts.title: Delhi's largest lake shrank 97%
facts.unit: sq km (Najafgarh Jheel, 1880s → today)
facts.interpretation: The Najafgarh Jheel once spread ~226 sq km across the Delhi-Haryana border before colonial-era drainage converted the Sahibi river into the Najafgarh drain. The ~7 sq km remnant is still the largest water body in the NCT (the 601-hectare polygon dominates Delhi's OSM water layer) - and its wetland-notification file has been stuck between two states since INTACH's 2014 petition.
facts.source_label: ThePrint - Najafgarh Jheel's wetland tag stuck 11 years

facts.title: The census counts 893 water bodies in the capital
facts.unit: water bodies (Jal Dharohar census, enumerated 2022)
facts.interpretation: India's first Census of Water Bodies enumerated 893 in NCT Delhi with ownership, capacity and encroachment attributes - the official denominator for every restoration claim in the city.
facts.source_label: 1st Water Bodies Census / Jal Dharohar (via OpenCity)

facts.title: 22 km of river carries ~80% of its pollution
facts.unit: of the Yamuna's pollution load, in the 2% of its length inside Delhi
facts.interpretation: The Wazirabad-to-Okhla stretch - 22 km of a 1,376-km river - contributes the bulk of the Yamuna's entire pollution load. Everything Delhi says about cleaning the river is a claim about these 22 km.

facts.title: Two drains deliver 84% of Delhi's Yamuna load
facts.unit: of Delhi's pollution load via Najafgarh + Shahdara drains
facts.interpretation: The Najafgarh drain alone carries roughly two-thirds of the city's sewage to the river; add the Shahdara drain and two channels account for 84% of Delhi's contribution. Trapping these two IS the clean-up, whatever else is announced.

facts.title: 37 sewage plants, a quarter of their capacity unused
facts.unit: STPs, 814 MGD installed capacity (~25% unused)
facts.interpretation: DJB operates 37 STPs with 814.26 MGD combined capacity, running around 744 MGD - while 22 drains still discharge into the Yamuna. Capacity exists on paper that the sewer network never delivers sewage to.
facts.source_label: ThePrint on Delhi Economic Survey STP figures

facts.title: 75% of Delhi's STPs lack disinfection equipment
facts.unit: of STPs without chlorination/UV/ozonation (DJB's own NGT filing)
facts.interpretation: In its sworn reply to NGT OA 183/2024, DJB conceded that three-quarters of its plants cannot disinfect effluent - meaning even 'treated' discharge can carry faecal bacteria to the river. The CAG separately found effluent from 25 STPs failing DPCC norms.
facts.source_label: DJB status report to NGT, OA 183/2024

facts.title: 212 MGD of colony sewage goes straight to storm drains
facts.unit: MGD untreated, from 1,080 unauthorised colonies (CAG)
facts.interpretation: The CAG found that sewage from 1,080 unauthorised colonies - more than a third of Delhi's total generation - was being dumped untreated into storm-water drains, which is how it reaches the Yamuna regardless of STP capacity.

facts.title: Half of Delhi's water earns no revenue
facts.unit: Non-Revenue Water; Rs 4,988 crore revenue impact (FY18-22)
facts.interpretation: The CAG's performance audit found NRW running at 51-53% of daily supply across the audit period, costing Rs 4,988 crore - the audited core of what popular discourse calls the tanker-mafia economy.

facts.title: DJB's debt mountain: Rs 66,595 crore
facts.unit: crore rupees outstanding loans + interest (March 2022)
facts.interpretation: The utility's accumulated loans and interest exceed a decade of its revenues; the CAG adds that its accounts, audited only to 2021-22, 'do not depict a true and fair picture'.

facts.title: Only 40% of the water DJB produces is ever billed
facts.unit: of production billed (371 MGD); only 66% of that on meters
facts.interpretation: In 2021-22 DJB billed 371 of the ~930+ MGD it produced, and only 244 MGD of the billed volume rested on actual meter readings - the arithmetic behind the NRW headline.

facts.title: Planning failures cost Delhi Rs 2,243 crore of ADB financing
facts.unit: crore rupees withdrawn by the Asian Development Bank
facts.interpretation: The CAG records that deficiencies in project conceptualisation led ADB to withdraw Rs 2,243 crore earmarked for rehabilitating the Wazirabad WTP and its command area - the city lost a funded fix for its oldest treatment complex.

facts.title: The state's own Economic Survey uses the word 'mafia'
facts.unit: of Delhi's water 'wasted or pilfered by tanker mafia'
facts.interpretation: Delhi's Economic Survey 2023-24 (Chapter 13) states that 52.35% of the city's water is wasted or pilfered by the tanker mafia - a government document adopting the accusation usually attributed to activists.

facts.title: 509 litres in Central Delhi, 29 in Mehrauli
facts.unit: gap in per-capita daily water availability across the city
facts.interpretation: Peer-reviewed analysis (Frontiers in Water, 2021) found per-capita availability ranging from 509 LPCD in Central Delhi to 29 LPCD in Mehrauli - the sharpest documented intra-city water inequality in any Indian metro.
facts.source_label: Frontiers in Water - Five Axes of Inequities

facts.title: Four DJB zones get less than a third of the water norm
facts.unit: GPCD in 4 zones; <40 in 8 zones, vs the 60 GPCD requirement
facts.interpretation: The CAG's zone-level numbers put official flesh on the inequity finding: four zones below 20 gallons per capita per day and eight below 40, against the 60 GPCD service norm.

facts.title: Asia's largest unauthorised colony runs on tankers
facts.unit: people on ~5 sq km in Sangam Vihar, ~80% tanker-dependent
facts.interpretation: Sangam Vihar packs around a million residents into five square kilometres without regular piped supply; most households buy water from tankers filled at private borewells - the retail face of the NRW economy.
facts.source_label: Down to Earth - Sangam Vihar tanker economy

facts.title: 675 JJ bastis, 306,521 households, on the official roster
facts.unit: jhuggi-jhopri clusters listed by DUSIB
facts.interpretation: DUSIB's own list names 675 JJ clusters totalling 306,521 households, with land-owning agency and constituency for each - an unusually complete official slum roster, and the denominator for any claim about serving Delhi's informal settlements.

facts.title: Delhi's structural water gap keeps widening
facts.unit: shortage against assessed requirement (CAG, FY22)
facts.interpretation: Raw-water shortage grew from 22% to 24% and potable shortage from 24.2% to 25.79% across the CAG's audit period - roughly 960 MGD produced against ~1,290+ assessed need, with the auditor calling augmentation prospects 'remote'.

facts.title: Delhi's water share rests on a 1994 'interim' MoU
facts.unit: BCM/year allocated to Delhi (~750 cusecs at peak)
facts.interpretation: Five states signed the upper-Yamuna MoU on 12 May 1994 as an interim seasonal allocation pending final apportionment. Three decades on, the interim paper is still the operative constitution of Delhi's water supply.

facts.title: 70% of Delhi's water arrives in one Haryana canal
facts.unit: km - the Munak carrier, ~700-1,050 cusecs
facts.interpretation: The Carrier-Lined Channel from Munak feeds five of Delhi's nine treatment plants. There is no public daily measurement of the single most important water conduit in the capital - its flows become public only when a crisis reaches court, as in June 2024.

facts.title: Delhi drinks from dams 240-400 km away
facts.unit: cusecs from Tehri (Uttarakhand); Bhakra share from ~240 km (HP/Punjab)
facts.interpretation: Tehri's drinking-water component earmarks 300 cusecs (~162 MGD) for Delhi via the Upper Ganga Canal, and a BBMB-resolved share of Bhakra storage rides the Western Yamuna Canal - a pumped-from-far city with no local runway at all.

facts.title: The capital pumps more groundwater than nature returns
facts.unit: stage of extraction (CGWB dynamic assessment)
facts.interpretation: NCT Delhi extracts beyond its annual recharge, with Najafgarh, Mehrauli and Alipur blocks classified Over-Exploited - and uniquely, the central groundwater regulator has no NOC jurisdiction here; extraction is governed by GNCTD orders.

facts.title: A third of Delhi's groundwater samples exceed salinity limits
facts.unit: of samples above the salinity threshold (CGWB 2024)
facts.interpretation: The Annual Ground Water Quality Report 2024 put Delhi among India's worst states for salinity exceedance, with elevated uranium, lead and nitrate in monitored wells - ~114 sq km of the south-west has no fresh groundwater at all.

facts.title: July 2023: the Yamuna's highest level in 45 years
facts.unit: metres at Old Railway Bridge (13 July 2023)
facts.interpretation: The river beat its 1978 record by 1.17 m, flooding the Ring Road and ITO. The CWC's own case study documents it; reporting fixed on the ITO barrage's three jammed gates as the proximate cause of the depth in central Delhi.

facts.title: India's flood forecasting was born on the Yamuna at Delhi
facts.unit: first CWC flood-forecast station (Old Railway Bridge)
facts.interpretation: The Central Water Commission's flood forecasting service began in 1958 with the Yamuna gauge at Delhi's Old Railway Bridge - 67 years of continuous flood record on the same river cross-section the city still watches every monsoon.
facts.source_label: CWC (FFS history in the 2023 case study)

facts.title: 3,737 km of drains, 11 agencies, one unimplemented plan
facts.unit: km of drainage across 201 natural + engineered channels
facts.interpretation: IIT Delhi's 2018 Drainage Master Plan mapped 426.5 km of natural and 3,311 km of engineered drains split across 11 agencies - and remains largely on paper eight years later, a finding every flood season re-verifies.

facts.title: India's first foreign-funded river clean-up started here in 1993
facts.unit: crore rupees spent in just 2017-2021; river still failing standards
facts.interpretation: The Yamuna Action Plan (JICA-funded from 1993) made the Yamuna India's first internationally financed river restoration. The CAG-era accounting shows ~Rs 6,857 crore spent in four recent years alone while the Delhi stretch stayed unfit for bathing - the spending-vs-outcome gap the dashboard exists to make legible.
facts.source_label: JICA - Yamuna Action Plan ex-post evaluation

facts.title: A court ruled the river too polluted to pray in
facts.unit: Delhi High Court order on Chhath at the Yamuna
facts.interpretation: In November 2024 the Delhi High Court declined to allow Chhath rituals on the Yamuna's banks, citing pollution - a judicial certification of the river's condition, delivered against the festival that most publicly depends on it. The toxic-froth images at Kalindi Kunj return every October-November.
facts.source_label: Business Standard - HC denies Chhath at Yamuna bank

facts.title: The Yamuna's great advocate died the day his parliament met
facts.unit: Manoj Misra's Yamuna Jiye Abhiyaan
facts.interpretation: Forester-turned-activist Manoj Misra founded Yamuna Jiye Abhiyaan in 2007 and won the NGT's landmark 'Maily se Nirmal' rejuvenation order (2015) in India's longest-running river docket. He died on 4 June 2023 - the same day a Yamuna Sansad convened in Delhi to demand the river's revival.
facts.source_label: Down to Earth - Manoj Misra obituary

facts.title: Delhi's biodiversity parks show restoration can work
facts.unit: acres - Yamuna Biodiversity Park (2002- ), DDA + Delhi University
facts.interpretation: The Yamuna Biodiversity Park rebuilt floodplain wetlands and grasslands on degraded land at Wazirabad, and the DDA's park network now claims recharge worth thousands of crores - the standing proof-of-concept for the floodplain the city still builds against.

facts.title: India's most ambitious water-heritage restoration is in Nizamuddin
facts.unit: core phase (work continuing) - Aga Khan Trust for Culture
facts.interpretation: AKTC's Nizamuddin renewal restored the dargah's 14th-century baoli and the water systems of Humayun's Tomb and Sunder Nursery, winning UNESCO Asia-Pacific awards in 2021 - proof that Delhi's historic water infrastructure can be brought back to working life.
